newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea seeks minister-level peace talks.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea seeks minister-level peace talks.

text.p: South Korea will seek talks at minister level with North Korea, the United States and China when their officials meet on Tuesday to arrange four-nation peace negotiations, Seoul officials said.

"In view of the importance of these talks, we believe it would be appropriate to have chief delegates at minister level and alternate chief delegates at vice minister-level," said foreign ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung.
"But we will be flexible as long as the talks could serve our purposes of solidifying peace on the Korean peninsula and building up mutual trust," he said.

Tuesday's meeting in New York is aimed at setting a date, venue and agenda for the opening of substantive negotiations, which Seoul and Washington want in September, to find an end to Cold War confrontation on the Korean peninsula.
It was expected to produce an important indication of Pyongyang's willingness for detente.
Many North Korea watchers said the hunger-stricken North had not abandoned its policy of taking the South by force and that it might have accepted peace talks to get much-needed food aid.
"Once peace talks get under way and the North shows sincerity for detente, we can discuss large-scale assistance to the North as part of confidence-building steps," Lee said.
He said he did not expect the North to agree to sign a peace treaty with the South quickly to replace the armistice that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
"But we want to make sure that any large-scale assistance will not be used as a means to re-allocate their own resources to strengthen their military," he added.
Seoul officials have said about a quarter of North Korea's gross national product was used to finance the North's 1.1 million-strong army, one of the world's largest.

"If it cuts five percent of its defence spendings, it could save about $300 million annually, which is enough to buy about two million tonnes of corn and end Pyongyang's food shortage," said one official at Seoul's unification ministry.

North Korea has demanded that Seoul and Washington provide food aid to compensate for starvation caused by devastating floods in 1995 and 1996 and a system that critics say is unable to meet the country's needs.

The United States and South Korea have supplied the North with tens of thousands of tonnes of emergency food to help ease hardship but have ruled out major assistance until the four nations start substantive negotiations for peace.
Washington officials said it is "entirely possible" that North Korea's sole reason for joining the peace talks is designed to derive maximum benefit for the regime.
"The four-party talks could well develop into a food-for-peace package," a Seoul foreign ministry official said.
United Nations agencies said on Monday recent drought in North Korea had plunged Pyongyang further towards famine.
They said 70 percent of maize crops had been ruined by North Korea's worst drought in over half a century.

"The crop is lost. It is absolutely disastrous. It is going to be a major catastrophe that no one realised because they kept on hoping it would rain tomorrow," said Roberto Christen, an adviser with the U.N.'s Rome-based Food and Agriculture Organisation.
He was part of a U.N.-coordinated mission to North Korea at the end of July to assess the effect of the drought.
